Choosing between a high-growth travel platform and a legacy retailer in transition requires balancing profitability against deep value. Is Airbnb Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) or GameStop Corp. (NYSE:GME) the better choice for your portfolio today?

Airbnb revolutionized the lodging market through its peer-to-peer network, while GameStop is navigating a shift from physical software to a digital-first entertainment model. Both companies have worked to streamline operations, yet they represent very different risk-reward profiles for everyday investors looking to allocate capital in the current market.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a global online marketplace that connects hosts with travelers looking for unique stays or local experiences. The company has established itself as a leader among travel and tourism stocks by offering an alternative to traditional hotels. By leveraging a network of over 5 million hosts to offer more than 9 million active listings, the business maintains a flexible platform that scales quickly. Note that Airbnb currently outsources a large majority of its community support operations to third-party providers.

In its latest annual report filed for FY 2025, revenue reached about $12.3 billion, representing growth of approximately 10.8% compared to the previous year. This expansion was supported by high net income of about $2.5 billion. The company reported a net margin of roughly 20.4%, which shows the percentage of revenue remaining as profit after all expenses are paid. While this was a slight decrease from the prior year, it remains a healthy figure for the travel services industry.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.3x. This ratio measures total debt relative to what shareholders own, suggesting the company maintains a conservative level of borrowing. Its current ratio, which tracks the ability to pay short-term bills using short-term assets, was close to 1.4x. Free cash flow for the period reached around $4.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since stock-based compensation is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for GameStop

GameStop serves as a specialty retailer for the gaming community, selling physical and digital games, collectibles, and hardware. The company operated approximately 2,206 leased stores as of late January 2026, while also pursuing additional sales through its e-commerce platforms. Its business model relies heavily on relationships with major manufacturers and publishers. In fiscal 2025, partners like Nintendo Co. (OTC:NTDOF), Sony Group Corp. (NYSE:SONY), and Pokémon accounted for a majority of the new products the company purchased.

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB)and Five Below (NASDAQ:FIVE)both compete for discretionary consumer dollars, but they do so through entirely different business models. Choosing between them requires weighing the digital scale against the physical retail expansion.

Airbnb dominates the alternative accommodation space with millions of active listings, while Five Below focuses on low-price, trend-right goods for kids and teens. Investors often compare them because both represent growth-oriented plays within the consumer cyclical sector, albeit with different risk profiles and capital requirements.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a global marketplace for travel and tourism stocks, connecting more than 5.5 million hosts with guests seeking short-term stays. The company has moved beyond simple lodging to include Experiences and property management tools through its Co-Host Network. Its business model is capital-light, as it does not own the properties on its platform and relies on Apple for critical app distribution.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $12.3 billion, representing growth of approximately 10.8% over the previous fiscal year. Net income for the same period was roughly $2.5 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 20.4%. This net margin, which measures how much profit a company keeps for every dollar of sales, reflects the high profitability inherent in a digital marketplace.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was roughly 1.4x, which measures a company's ability to cover short-term debts with its current assets. The debt-to-equity ratio was close to 0.3x, indicating a conservative level of debt relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was nearly $4.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow.

The case for Five Below

Five Below is a value retailer that organizes its stores into eight distinct "worlds," such as Style, Tech, and Candy. The company targets kids, pre-teens, and value-oriented shoppers, operating over 1,900 stores across 46 states. It is a prominent name among retail stocks because of its ability to quickly capitalize on viral trends while maintaining low price points for its core demographic.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $4.8 billion, representing nearly 22.9% growth over the prior year. Net income for the fiscal period was close to $358.6 million, and the company reported a net margin of roughly 7.5%. While lower than software-based businesses, this margin reflects the costs of sourcing physical inventory and managing a vast network of brick-and-mortar locations.

As digital platforms reshape global consumption, investors often weigh high-margin services against capital-intensive retail. Deciding between Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) and Coupang (NYSE:CPNG) requires balancing global reach against regional logistics dominance.

Airbnb connects hosts and travelers worldwide through a capital-light marketplace, while Coupang operates a massive end-to-end delivery network across South Korea and Taiwan. Both companies lead their respective niches but face vastly different operational hurdles. This comparison evaluates their growth, profitability, and risk profiles to help you determine which stock fits your strategy.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a global marketplace that connects more than 5.5 million hosts with travelers seeking unique accommodations and experiences. As detailed in its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, the company utilizes a capital-light model that scales rapidly across 220 countries and regions. Recent initiatives like the Co-Host Network and redesigned service offerings aim to attract more inventory and enhance guest satisfaction.

In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $12.3 billion, representing growth of 10.8% over the prior year. The company reported net income of $2.5 billion, resulting in a net margin of 20.4%. This performance follows a period of high profitability in previous years, although the net margin slightly decreased from 23.9% in FY 2024.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.3x, which indicates that the company uses a conservative amount of debt relative to its shareholder equity. Its current ratio of nearly 1.4x measures the company's ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets. Free cash flow, calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, reached $4.6 billion, though stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 34.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Coupang

Coupang is a dominant force in the South Korean e-commerce market, providing retail, restaurant delivery, and fintech services through its integrated logistics network. The company is a prominent name among retail stocks due to its WOW membership program and rapid delivery speeds. To broaden its reach, Coupang has expanded into Taiwan and recently acquired Farfetch to bolster its presence in the global luxury fashion market.

Airbnb acts as a dominant platform for alternative accommodations and experiences, whereas Chewy serves as a dedicated digital ecosystem for pet products and healthcare. Both companies rely on consumer discretionary spending but face vastly different competitive landscapes and regulatory environments.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a peer-to-peer marketplace that connects over 5 million hosts with guests seeking unique travel experiences. The company does not own the properties on its platform, which allows it to scale quickly as more hosts join the travel and tourism stocks ecosystem. It focuses on integrating artificial intelligence to personalize search results and has developed partnerships with major cultural and sports organizations to keep its brand relevant.

In FY 2025, revenue reached about $12.3 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 11% compared to the previous year. The company reported a net income of roughly $2.5 billion for the period. While net income remained strong, its net margin, which shows how much of each dollar of revenue becomes profit, came in at about 20.4%, down slightly from the previous fiscal year.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Airbnb maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.3x. This ratio compares a company's total debt to its shareholder equity, with lower numbers generally indicating less financial risk. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, was close to 1.4x. Free cash flow reached about $4.6 billion, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 34% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since stock-based compensation is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Chewy

Chewy serves as a leading e-commerce destination for pet owners in the United States and Canada, offering roughly 190,000 different products. Its strategy centers on the Autoship subscription program, which provides predictable revenue and high customer loyalty. Recently, the company has expanded its reach into pet health through Chewy Pharmacy and Chewy Vet Care clinics, including the strategic acquisition of Modern Animal.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $12.6 billion, which was an increase of about 6.2% over the prior year. The company generated a net income of around $222.8 million. Its net margin was approximately 1.8%, reflecting the competitive nature of retail, where high volumes are often balanced by narrower profit figures per sale.

Growth investors focus on stocks that are seeing above-average financial growth, as this feature helps these securities garner the market's attention and deliver solid returns. But finding a growth stock that can live up to its true potential can be a tough task.

In addition to volatility, these stocks carry above-average risk by their very nature. Also, one could end up losing from a stock whose growth story is actually over or nearing its end.

However, the Zacks Growth Style Score (part of the Zacks Style Scores system), which looks beyond the traditional growth attributes to analyze a company's real growth prospects, makes it pretty easy to find cutting-edge growth stocks.

Airbnb, Inc. (ABNB) is on the list of such stocks currently recommended by our proprietary system. In addition to a favorable Growth Score, it carries a top Zacks Rank.

Studies have shown that stocks with the best growth features consistently outperform the market. And for stocks that have a combination of a Growth Score of A or B and a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) or 2 (Buy), returns are even better.

While there are numerous reasons why the stock of this company is a great growth pick right now, we have highlighted three of the most important factors below:

Earnings Growth

Earnings growth is arguably the most important factor, as stocks exhibiting exceptionally surging profit levels tend to attract the attention of most investors. For growth investors, double-digit earnings growth is highly preferable, as it is often perceived as an indication of strong prospects (and stock price gains) for the company under consideration.

While the historical EPS growth rate for Airbnb is 22.8%, investors should actually focus on the projected growth. The company's EPS is expected to grow 31.2% this year, crushing the industry average, which calls for EPS growth of 28.3%.

Impressive Asset Utilization Ratio

Asset utilization ratio -- also known as sales-to-total-assets (S/TA) ratio -- is often overlooked by investors, but it is an important indicator in growth investing. This metric shows how efficiently a firm is utilizing its assets to generate sales.

Right now, Airbnb has an S/TA ratio of 0.52, which means that the company gets $0.52 in sales for each dollar in assets. Comparing this to the industry average of 0.51, it can be said that the company is more efficient.

While the level of efficiency in generating sales matters a lot, so does the sales growth of a company. And Airbnb is well positioned from a sales growth perspective too. The company's sales are expected to grow 15.8% this year versus the industry average of 3.2%.
